data.title: Betamethasone (oral)
data.summary: VII Systemic corticosteroids · Long-acting fluorinated glucocorticoid (biological half-life 36–54 h)
data.body:
_Oral · VII Systemic corticosteroids_

**Class:** Long-acting fluorinated glucocorticoid (biological half-life 36–54 h)

## Mechanism of action
- Glucocorticoid receptor agonist like prednisolone, but much more potent and longer acting
- No mineralocorticoid effect

## Pharmacokinetics
- Equivalence: 0.6 mg betamethasone ≈ 5 mg prednisolone (about 25 times hydrocortisone)
- Crosses the placenta (not inactivated by 11β-HSD2) — used to mature fetal lungs

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Oral mini-pulse (OMP): progressive/unstable vitiligo, spreading alopecia areata, extensive lichen planus
- General systemic steroid indications (less often than prednisolone)

## Dose & formulations
- OMP (Pasricha regimen): 5 mg betamethasone (or dexamethasone) as a single morning dose on 2 consecutive days per week (adults); children 0.1 mg/kg on the same schedule
- Continue OMP for about 3–6 months for vitiligo, then taper
- Tablets 0.5 mg (and 1 mg in some brands)

## Adverse effects
- Same as systemic steroids; with OMP mainly weight gain, acne, insomnia, menstrual disturbance, mild Cushingoid features
- Long-acting steroids suppress the HPA axis more than prednisolone if given daily

## Contraindications
- As for systemic steroids

## Drug interactions
- As for prednisolone

## Monitoring
- Weight, BP, glucose during OMP

## Pregnancy & lactation
Crosses the placenta (used deliberately for fetal lung maturity); avoid for skin disease in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- OMP — pulse dosing on 2 days a week reduces side effects but still stops disease activity
- Long-acting: more HPA suppression if given daily
- Not inactivated by the placenta (unlike prednisolone)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.8 (Table 8.2, OMP indications); Wolverton 4e ch.13. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
